title: I1 — Level-2 capacity cannot sustain the incoming workload
evidenceType: Measured in Exercise 3; capacity requirement also calculated
evidence: Exercise 3 baseline run b46e0b16-c3fa-49f4-ba82-83c209073349: 4 arrivals/hour, Level-1/Level-2 capacities 5/3, 720-hour admission horizon and 20 replications. Mean cycle 1063.69 hours; Level-2 utilization 97.37%, mean queue 1166.92. Expected Level-2 work is 156 minutes per incoming case, or 10.4 staff-hours/hour. These are finite-horizon results including backlog drain, not steady-state waits.
change: Validate and provision sufficient qualified Level-2 capacity; use 12 as a candidate at the original demand and routing, and reassess staffing after redesign.
justification: Available capacity is below the workload even before considering variability. At 5/12, the measured mean cycle falls to 23.81 hours and Level-2 mean queue to 2.25 requests. Capacity relief directly addresses this bottleneck.
tradeoff: The fully staffed hourly budget rises from €380 at 5/3 to €920 at 5/12. This differs from processing labor cost per case. No service-level target or staffing budget establishes a unique optimum.
validation: Use the completed 3, 6, 9, 11, 12, 15 Level-2 capacity comparisons. Retest candidate capacities after changing routing or tasks; assess mean/p95 cycle, queues and hourly staffing budget.

title: I2 — Internal pickup delays dominate the as-is elapsed time
evidenceType: Assignment assumption; causes and achievable savings need validation
evidence: Assignment assumptions: 1 hour before checking, 2 hours before evaluation, 20 hours before resolution work and 20 hours before Level-1 fetches the written result. With the given probabilities and repeat visits, these contribute 42.6 expected hours per initial request in Exercise 1. Exercise 3 explicitly removes these fixed delays; it cannot measure a further reduction of them.
change: Introduce event-driven work assignment and notifications instead of periodic/manual pickup; instrument queue entry, assignment and start times.
justification: Prompt dispatch can remove avoidable polling or batch-release time. Real resource queues must remain in the model, because an alert cannot create missing staff capacity.
tradeoff: The assignment does not establish how much of each observed delay is polling versus staff shortage. Removing all delays is an upper-bound scenario, not a demonstrated benefit. Avoid adding observed waits on top of modeled queues without separating their causes.
validation: Use a separate Exercise-1-based timing scenario for fixed-delay sensitivity, retaining the client delay. In an operational pilot measure dispatch latency separately from resource waiting. Do not claim these savings from the Exercise 3 comparison.

title: I3 — Written resolutions pass through an avoidable Level-1 relay
evidenceType: Assignment process structure; benefit is a proposal
evidence: The assignment routes a Level-2 written resolution back through Level-1, which spends 20 minutes sending it to the client. If unsuccessful, Level-1 spends another 2 minutes forwarding it back. Both occur on the repeated resolution path; the known-resolution branch is a different activity.
change: After Level-2 completes the resolution, notify the client automatically and route unsuccessful feedback directly to the appropriate Level-2 queue. Retain a named contact and an exception path for cases needing explanation.
justification: Eliminating duplicate forwarding reduces work and transfers while preserving diagnosis, resolution and client confirmation. Automating delivery targets the relay rather than the problem-solving task.
tradeoff: The relay may contain useful explanation, so validate which requests can bypass it. Assign automation latency and operating cost explicitly; do not assume all technical work is free.
validation: In a separate to-be model replace only the post-writing Send resolution and failed-feedback forwarding steps. Hold staffing and probabilities constant first; compare labor cost, cycle time and communication quality.

title: I4 — Eighty percent of incoming requests require escalation
evidenceType: Assignment routing probability; improvement is conditional
evidence: The supplied known-resolution probability is 20%, so 80% of initial requests reach Level-2. At 4 requests/hour this means 3.2 new Level-2 requests/hour before repeated attempts. The assignment describes Level-1 staff as junior; it does not establish that they are underperforming.
change: Broaden Level-1 competence through targeted training and a maintained knowledge base, while retaining escalation for difficult or uncertain cases.
justification: Broader skills can allow genuinely suitable requests to finish at Level-1 and reduce specialist demand. Under unchanged task times and rework, moving the known rate from 20% to 40% would reduce expected Level-2 workload from 10.4 to 7.8 staff-hours/hour; this is a conditional calculation.
tradeoff: Training, knowledge maintenance and longer initial checking consume effort. The 40% known rate is a proposed sensitivity value, not a measured improvement; monitor incorrect closures.
validation: Test known/unknown pairs 0.2/0.8, 0.3/0.7 and 0.4/0.6 together, always summing to one. Include added checking/training effort and check quality before adopting new probabilities.

title: I5 — Unsuccessful resolutions create repeated work and client delays
evidenceType: Assignment failure rate; validation effect unmeasured
evidence: The assignment uses a 20% unsuccessful-resolution probability on each attempt. Given escalation and a constant independent retry probability, expected attempts are 1/(1−0.2)=1.25. Each retry repeats resolution, writing, delivery and a client-response wait; evaluation is not repeated in the supplied model.
change: Add a proportionate validation/checklist step before delivery, with effort targeted to the likely causes of failure.
justification: An output check may reduce failed deliveries and repeat work. It must be justified against its added processing cost and potential pressure on the same Level-2 pool.
tradeoff: Extra checking can make an overloaded queue worse. A reduced failure probability is unverified and must be paired with the added validation duration and resource consumption.
validation: Test paired assumptions such as validation times 0, 5, 10 minutes and failure rates 0.20, 0.15, 0.10; maintain solved=1−failed. Compare total labor cost, mean/p95 cycle and observed quality. Treat each pair as a hypothesis.

title: I6 — Client feedback imposes a long external wait
evidenceType: Assignment delay and Exercise 3 result; proposed reduction unmeasured
evidence: The assignment specifies a 20-hour client response delay per delivered resolution. It is retained in Exercise 3 as an unresourced 1200-minute wait. At 80% escalation and 20% rework, expected response-wait visits per initial case are 0.8/(1−0.2)=1, contributing about 20 hours to the mean cycle. The 5/12 mean cycle is 23.81 hours.
change: Provide a direct test-result submission channel with clear instructions and proportionate reminders; route the result automatically to closure or rework.
justification: Integrating client feedback into the workflow can reduce avoidable response friction. Once staffing is sufficient, this external wait is the main remaining elapsed-time component.
tradeoff: Customer availability and test duration are not controlled by the helpdesk. Reminders may not shorten them. Preserve human confirmation; do not assume silence means success.
validation: Test response delays of 20, 10 and 5 hours as explicit sensitivity assumptions, then measure actual response times in a pilot. Do not report the lower delays as achieved benefits.
